title: Constructive Algorithm for Sequence Game Reconstruction
approach_explanation: The problem requires us to reconstruct an original sequence $a$ given a filtered sequence $b$. The sequence $b$ is formed by keeping $a_1$ and every subsequent element $a_i$ where $a_{i-1}  ge a_i$ is false (i.e., $a_{i-1}  leq a_i$). To reverse-engineer this, we iterate through $b$. We always include $b_i$. If $b_i  ge b_{i-1}$, it means $b_i$ could naturally follow $b_{i-1}$ in $a$. However, if $b_i < b_{i-1}$, a drop occurs in $b$. In the original sequence $a$, such a drop must be preceded by an element greater than or equal to $b_{i-1}$ and followed by $b_i$. To safely satisfy the condition and prevent $b_i$ from being falsely filtered out when compared to a higher preceding element, we can insert $b_i$ twice (or insert a small number like 1, or $b_i$ itself). Specifically, inserting $b_i$ twice ensures that the first copy drops from $b_{i-1}$ (so it won't be in $b$) and the second copy is equal to the first, satisfying $a_{i-1}  leq a_i$ so it is kept in $b$. This guarantees exact reconstruction of $b$ when the game rules are applied to $a$.

code_breakdown.explanation: Reads the number of test cases $t$, and for each test case reads the sequence length $n$ and the sequence $b$ of size $n$.

Initializes an array $a$ starting with $b[0]$. Iterates from index $1$ to $n-1$. If $b[i]  ge b[i-1]$, pushes $b[i]$ to $a$. If $b[i] < b[i-1]$, pushes $b[i]$ twice to $a$, handling the non-increasing transition safely.
Prints the size of the constructed sequence $a$, followed by all elements separated by spaces.

complexity_analysis.time_justification: For each test case, we iterate through the sequence $b$ of length $n$ a single time, performing $O(1)$ operations per element. Across all test cases, the sum of $n$ is bounded by $2  cdot 10^5$, leading to an optimal linear time complexity of $O(∑ n)$.
complexity_analysis.space_justification: We store the input vector $b$ of size $n$ and the constructed vector $a$ of size at most $2n$. Thus, the auxiliary space complexity is linear with respect to the input size $n$.

strengths: Simple, elegant, and directly addresses the construction constraint without unnecessary complexity.
Handles non-decreasing and decreasing consecutive elements correctly.
Meets the length requirement $n  leq m  leq 2n$.
edge_cases_handled: Strictly decreasing sequences where every element triggers the duplication rule.
Non-decreasing sequences where no elements need duplication.

optimization_and_alternatives.tradeoffs: Instead of dynamic `push_back` which can occasionally trigger reallocations, we can pre-allocate maximum possible capacity ($2n$) for vector $a$ and use an index pointer, slightly reducing overhead.
